items: Scientific investigation means learning how to FIND new facts: ask focused questions, design simple experiments and use observations to improve understanding — keeping the feet on careful observation (root) while ideas fly with creative thinking (kite).
Investigation = learning how to find new facts, not just learning facts.
Investigators observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully and explain clearly.
Balance the root (careful observation) with the kite (creative thinking).

This year's investigation goes from tiny microbes we cannot see to planet-wide challenges we cannot ignore — and each stop leads to the next: microbes and health → electricity, force and pressure → particles and materials → light, Moon and calendars → life on Earth and climate.
From tiny microbes to planet-wide challenges.

notes.h: Planning an Investigation: What to Change, What to Observe
items: To investigate an everyday wonder like a puffing puri, turn it into a scientific question, then plan two lists: the things we can change or control, and the things we can observe or measure.
Science is everywhere — the kitchen is a lab.
Turn a wonder into a scientific question.
Plan two lists: what we change, what we observe — yes/no or a number.

notes.h: Fair Testing: Change One Thing at a Time
items: Change only one thing at a time and keep everything else the same, note everything you see and sense, and let the results raise new questions — this is systematic investigation, the way all scientific experiments are done.
Change ONE thing, keep the rest the same.
Note everything you see and sense.
Every round of experiments brings new questions — that is systematic investigation.
Wrong: Science is only remembering the facts in a book. Right: We learn facts AND learn how to find new facts — by focused questions, experiments and observations
Wrong: All microbes are harmful. Right: Some are invisible helpers (digesting food, making medicines); others cause infections
Wrong: You need a fancy laboratory to do science. Right: Science is everywhere; your kitchen is a wonderful place to observe and experiment
Wrong: Changing many things at once saves time and works just as well. Right: If two things change, we cannot tell which one made the difference — change one thing at a time

sol_items: What may change the way a puri puffs up when fried: The thickness of the dough, oil temperature, softness of the dough, size of the puri and pricking a hole.
How can we do a fair test?: Change only one thing and keep all other conditions the same.
imp_items: What are the three things an investigator does?
Observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully, explain clearly.
What does the kite on the right-hand pages remind us of?
Curiosity must take flight — ideas soaring with creative thinking.
Is 'time taken to puff' something we change or something we measure?
Something we measure (in seconds).
Give two things we can control when frying a puri.
Any two: dough thickness or size, flour kind, oil temperature, way of dropping.
You want to test whether atta or maida puris puff faster. What must you keep the same?
Dough thickness and size, oil temperature and the way of dropping.
Why keep notes of smell or smoke when you are measuring time?
Unexpected observations can explain results and lead to new questions.

notes.h: How We See the Invisible — Lens to Microscope
items: Our eyes cannot see very small things. Curved glass (a lens) makes things look bigger; better lenses became microscopes, which showed cells (Hooke) and tiny living beings (Leeuwenhoek).
Lens = lentil-shaped curved glass.
Hooke (1665) named the 'cell'.
Leeuwenhoek = Father of Microbiology (first saw bacteria).
Microscopes opened up a hidden living world.

notes.h: Parts of a Cell — Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
items: All living beings are made of cells. Onion peel and cheek cells show three basic parts — cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus — each with its own job.
Three basic parts: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus.
Membrane = boundary and gate; cytoplasm = where work happens; nucleus = controls activities and growth.
Onion cells have an extra cell wall.

notes.h: Plant Cell vs Animal Cell — Cell Wall, Plastids, Vacuole
items: Plant cells have the three basic parts plus a cell wall, plastids and a large vacuole; animal cells have no cell wall or plastids and small or no vacuoles.
A cell is not a simple bag of liquid — each part has a job.
Plant extras: cell wall, plastids, large vacuole.

notes.h: Variation in Shape and Structure of Cells
items: Cells differ in shape, size and structure, and each shape helps the cell do its own job; different cells work together, as in digestion.
The shape, size and structure of a cell help it carry out its specific function.
The number of cells also varies from organism to organism.

notes.h: Levels of Organisation — Cell to Organism
items: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, and organ systems make a complete organism. A multicellular organism starts as one cell, the egg.
Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism.
Life of a complex organism begins as one cell — the egg.
Microorganisms (microbes) are living beings of one or a few cells, too small to see without a microscope — protozoa, algae, fungi and bacteria. They live everywhere.
Microbes = too small for the naked eye; seen with a microscope (100–400×).
Four groups: protozoa, algae, fungi, bacteria.
Found everywhere.

notes.h: Key Players in Cleaning the Environment — Decomposition
items: Fungi and bacteria break down plant waste, dead animals and dung into simple, nutrient-rich substances (decomposition), making manure and returning nutrients to the soil.
Microbes = nature's recyclers.
Without them, waste and dead bodies would pile up and soil would lose nutrients.

notes.h: Microorganisms and Food — Yeast and Lactobacillus
items: Yeast (a fungus) breaks down sugar and gives carbon dioxide and a little alcohol — the dough rises. Lactobacillus (a bacterium) turns milk sugar into lactic acid — milk becomes sour curd. Both work best when warm.
Yeast → CO₂ (rise) + alcohol (smell).
Lactobacillus → lactic acid (sour curd).
Warmth helps both; sugar is their food.

notes.h: Rhizobium — Bacteria That Feed Nitrogen to Plants
items: Rhizobium bacteria live in swollen root nodules of legumes (beans, peas, lentils), trap nitrogen from the air and make it useful for the plant, so legumes need no chemical nitrogen fertiliser and enrich the soil.
Rhizobium → root nodules of legumes → nitrogen from air → healthy soil.
Crop rotation with legumes keeps soil fertile.

notes.h: Amazing Microalgae — Tiny Helpers in Water
items: Microalgae are microscopic plant-like organisms that make food using sunlight, release more than half of Earth's oxygen, feed aquatic animals, give supplements like Spirulina, clean water and make biofuel — so they must be conserved.
Microalgae: sunlight → food + oxygen.
Spirulina is rich in protein and B12.
Conserve microalgae.

notes.h: Unicellular and Multicellular — Why the Cell Is the Basic Unit of Life
items: Every organism is made of cells — one cell (unicellular) or many cells (multicellular). That is why the cell is the basic unit of life. Cells of microbes differ: fungi have a cell wall but no chloroplasts; bacteria have a nucleoid instead of a proper nucleus.
Cell = basic unit of life: every organism is made of one or more cells.
Unicellular: one cell does all. Multicellular: cells specialise and cooperate.
Wrong: A magnifying glass or microscope makes the object itself bigger. Right: Only the image looks bigger; the object stays the same size
Wrong: The cell membrane is a solid wall that lets nothing in or out. Right: It is porous — it lets needed materials in and waste out
Wrong: Animal cells also have a cell wall. Right: Animal cells have only a cell membrane as the outer layer; the cell wall is extra in plant cells
Wrong: All cells in the body have the same shape. Right: Cells are round, flat, spindle, long and branched … each shape suits its job
Wrong: A tissue is a group of all kinds of different cells. Right: A tissue is a group of SIMILAR cells; an organ has different tissues
Wrong: All microorganisms are made of just one cell. Right: Bacteria and Amoeba are one cell, but some fungi and algae are many-celled

sol_items: How do reading glasses and a magnifying glass help us s...: They have lenses that make things look bigger.
Which discovery helped us see the tiny world for the fi...: The microscope.
Onion peel cells and a brick wall: Cells are packed together like bricks in a wall.
Importance of the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nuc: The membrane controls what goes in and out; the cytoplasm holds the parts of the cell; the nucleus controls the cell's activities.
Muscle and nerve cells: Yes. Muscle cells are long and contract; nerve cells have long branches that carry signals.
Where did the microbes on rotting fruit come from?: From the air, soil and our hands; they land on the fruit and multiply.
imp_items: What is Organism?
Every living being, plant or animal, is called an organism.
What is Cell?
The basic unit of life — all living beings are made up of cells.

topics: What Is Health?
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease
Healthy Lifestyle
Our health depends on our lifestyle (how we live) and our environment
Clean Environment and Health
A clean environment — clean self, clean surroundings, clean air and water — keeps us healthy, while dirt, flies, mosquitos and ...
Symptoms and Signs
When something inside us is not working as it should, we show symptoms (what we feel, like pain) and signs (what can be seen or ...
Types of Diseases
A disease affects the normal working of the body or mind
Communicable Diseases — Cause and Spread
All communicable diseases are caused by pathogens
Non-communicable Diseases
Non-communicable diseases are not caused by germs: lifestyle-related diseases (obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer, ...
Immunity and Vaccines

Treatment of Diseases — Antibiotics and Other Therapies

Antibiotic Resistance
Indiscriminate use of antibiotics has made them less effective

items: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. A healthy person works efficiently, copes with difficult situations and adjusts well with others.
Health = physical + mental + social well-being
Not being sick is not enough to be healthy
A healthy person works efficiently, copes with difficulties and adjusts well with peers and society
Health and happiness are closely related — being happy helps us stay active and healthy, and good health improves mood (Snapshots)

Our health depends on our lifestyle (how we live) and our environment. Good daily habits — balanced diet, activity, enough sleep, less screen time, yoga, and saying NO to harmful substances — keep body and mind healthy.
Health depends on lifestyle and environment
Healthy habits support a healthy body and a healthy mind
Say NO to tobacco, alcohol and drugs

A clean environment — clean self, clean surroundings, clean air and water — keeps us healthy, while dirt, flies, mosquitos and polluted air make people fall sick. Feelings and relationships are part of a healthy environment too.
Clean self + clean surroundings + clean air and water
AQI tells how clean the air is
Talking, laughing and time with friends and family keep the mind healthy

When something inside us is not working as it should, we show symptoms (what we feel, like pain) and signs (what can be seen or measured, like high body temperature). Both help doctors understand what is making us unwell.
Symptom = felt
Sign = seen or measured
Doctors use both to find what is making us unwell

A disease affects the normal working of the body or mind. By cause and spread, diseases are communicable (caused by pathogens, spread from person to person) or non-communicable (not caused by pathogens, do not spread; linked to lifestyle, diet, environment). By duration, some are short-lasting and some chronic.
Ask: is a pathogen the cause? Yes → communicable; No → non-communicable
Diseases are not always caused by infections
Chronic = lasts more than 3 months

All communicable diseases are caused by pathogens. They spread through air (coughing, sneezing), direct contact, indirect contact (shared items), contaminated food and water, and insects called vectors. Knowing the route tells us how to prevent each disease. Good sanitation (toilets, no open defecation) blocks the food-and-water route.
Pathogen → route → new host
Routes: air · contact · food and water · vectors
Route decides prevention: mask for air, boiled water for water, nets for mosquitos

Non-communicable diseases are not caused by germs: lifestyle-related diseases (obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer, asthma) come from lifestyle, diet and environment; deficiency diseases (scurvy, anaemia, goitre) from lack of a nutrient. Many last more than 3 months (chronic). They are the most common cause of death in India and can often be prevented by healthy habits.
NCD = not caused by germs, does not spread
Lifestyle-related + deficiency diseases
Chronic = more than 3 months
Prevent with balanced diet, exercise, no tobacco

Our body's natural ability to fight diseases is immunity, run by the immune system. Protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine is acquired immunity. Vaccines train the immune system to recognise germs; they prevent disease but do not cure it.
Prevention is better than cure
Immunity = body's natural ability to fight disease
Vaccine → trained immune system → acquired immunity
Vaccines are preventive, not curative; they protect you and others, infants to elderly

notes.h: Treatment of Diseases — Antibiotics and Other Therapies
items: If the immune system fails we need treatment. Antibiotics kill bacteria by targeting parts of bacterial cells that differ from our cells — they do not work against viruses or protozoa. Traditional systems (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) help some conditions; NCDs are managed by medication, lifestyle change and rehabilitation, with early diagnosis and continuous care.
Antibiotics kill bacteria only
Not for viral infections like cold, cough, flu
NCDs are managed — early diagnosis, continuous care

Indiscriminate use of antibiotics has made them less effective. Antibiotic resistance is when bacteria that were once killed by an antibiotic survive and multiply despite it. Resistant bacteria spread through people, hospitals, animals, food and soil. We must use antibiotics only when prescribed, in the right dose, for the full duration.
Bacteria become resistant — not the person
Misuse: without prescription, incomplete dose, in animals
Use only on prescription, correct dose, full duration
Wrong: If I am not sick, I am healthy. Right: Health also needs mental and social well-being, not just absence of disease
Wrong: Skipping breakfast is harmless if I eat more at lunch. Right: Skipping meals, especially breakfast, is listed as a habit not good for health
Wrong: If I keep my body clean, dirty surroundings do not matter. Right: Dirty surroundings breed flies and mosquitos; people there fall sick more often
Wrong: Symptoms and signs are the same thing. Right: A symptom is felt by the patient; a sign can be seen or measured by others
Wrong: All diseases are caused by germs. Right: Non-communicable diseases like diabetes and asthma are not caused by pathogens
Wrong: The mosquito itself causes malaria. Right: Malaria is caused by protozoa; the mosquito is only the vector that carries them

sol_items: Group: Communicable: cold and flu, typhoid, chickenpox; non-communicable: diabetes, asthma.
Which are non-communicable among typhoid, asthma, diabe...: Asthma and diabetes.
Flu outbreak in school: Stay at home when sick, cover the mouth when coughing, wash hands, keep the classroom clean, and be kind to the ill classmate.
Travelling to a malaria area: Use mosquito nets and repellent, wear full sleeves, avoid stagnant water, and see a doctor if fever starts.
Uncle started smoking to fit in: Smoking harms the lungs and heart and is addictive; true friends accept a refusal.
Why is "antibiotics cure any infection" wrong?: Antibiotics work only on bacteria, not on viruses.
imp_items: Name the three aspects of health.
Physical, mental and social well-being.
Why is it hard to breathe in a smoky place?
Clean air is needed for health; smoke and dust pollute the air we breathe.
Is a rash a sign or a symptom?
A sign — it can be seen.
Which two of typhoid, asthma, diabetes, measles are non-communicable?
Asthma and diabetes.
Which of these spread through contaminated water: Hepatitis A, TB, Cholera, Chickenpox?
Hepatitis A and cholera.
Why should we not take an antibiotic for flu?
Flu is caused by a virus; antibiotics only act on parts of bacterial cells.

items: A wire carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field around it, so a compass needle near it deflects; the field disappears when the current stops.
Current ON → magnetic field → compass deflects
Current OFF → field disappears → needle returns
Oersted found this link in 1820

A coil of insulated wire carrying current behaves as a magnet — an electromagnet. An iron core inside makes it much stronger, and it loses its magnetism when the current stops, so it is a temporary magnet.
Coil + current = magnet
Iron core → much stronger
No current → no magnet (temporary)

notes.h: Poles and Strength of an Electromagnet
items: An electromagnet has a North and a South pole at its two ends; reversing the current reverses the poles. It becomes stronger with more current (more cells), more turns of the coil, and an iron core.
Two poles: N and S
Strength: current, number of turns, iron core
Poles: direction of current

Lifting electromagnets are strong electromagnets hung from cranes: current ON lifts iron and steel objects, current OFF releases them. They move, lift and sort heavy metal items in factories and scrap yards.
ON → lifts iron/steel
OFF → field disappears → load released
Used in factories and scrap yards

When an electric current passes through a conductor, the conductor gets heated: its resistance turns some electrical energy into heat. The heat depends on the current, material, thickness, length of the wire and the time the current flows.
Resistance → electrical energy → heat
More current → more heat
Heat depends on current, material, thickness, length, time

notes.h: Uses and Dangers of the Heating Effect
items: Heating appliances contain a heating element — a rod or coil of wire that gets hot when current flows. The same effect can waste energy in wires and overheat plugs and sockets, so we use rated wires and safety devices.
Heating element = rod/coil of high-resistance wire
Useful: appliances, lamp, furnace
Harmful: energy loss, overheating, fire — use rated wires, safety devices

A Voltaic (Galvanic) cell has two rods of different metals (electrodes) partly dipped in an electrolyte; a chemical reaction between them produces electricity. When the chemicals are used up, the cell is 'dead'.
Cell = 2 different metals + electrolyte
Chemical reaction → electricity
Chemicals used up → dead cell

The dry cell, one of the most widely used cells today, has a thick moist paste as electrolyte instead of a liquid. Its zinc container is the negative terminal and the carbon rod with a metal cap is the positive terminal. It is a single-use cell.
'Dry' = paste electrolyte
Zinc can (−), carbon rod + cap (+)
Single use

Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times, which prevents waste and saves money; they power watches, phones, laptops, cameras, inverters and vehicles, but slowly wear out. Used batteries should go to e-waste recycling.
Recharge and reuse many times — less waste, saves money
Wears out slowly
Li-ion most common; recycle as e-waste
Wrong: Electricity and magnetism have nothing to do with each other. Right: A current always produces a magnetic field around the wire
Wrong: An electromagnet needs a magnet hidden inside it. Right: There is no magnet — the current in the coil makes the magnetism
Wrong: If the compass's north pole is attracted to an end, that end is a north pole. Right: Unlike poles attract, so that end is a SOUTH pole
Wrong: A permanent magnet would be just as good on a crane. Right: It could not drop the load — the electromagnet releases it when the current is switched OFF
Wrong: Only special heater wires get hot. Right: Every conductor carrying current gets heated, some more than others
Wrong: Nichrome is used in heaters because it is a good conductor or cheaper than copper. Right: It is used because it generates more heat for a given current

sol_items: A current-carrying coil behaves like a ___: Magnet (an electromagnet).
Dry cells are less portable than Voltaic cells: False; dry cells are more portable.
An electromagnet with one cell attracts more clips than...: False; more cells give a stronger magnet.
Current through a nichrome wire: it warms; a compass be...: Both are correct: heating effect and magnetic effect.
Why is nichrome used in heating devices?: It produces more heat for a given current and does not oxidise easily.
Why are electric heaters more convenient than fire: They are cleaner and safer, with no smoke and no cutting of trees.
imp_items: How can we make a magnet that can be switched off?
Wind insulated wire around an iron nail and pass current through it.
How can the poles of an electromagnet be reversed?
By changing the direction of the current (swapping the cell's connections).
Why does a crane's electromagnet drop the scrap when the operator switches it off?
With no current there is no magnetic field, so the iron is no longer attracted.
Why does a nichrome wire get warmer than a copper wire of the same size?
Nichrome offers more resistance, so more electrical energy becomes heat.
Why is nichrome used in the heating element of an electric iron?
It generates more heat for a given current (higher resistance).
In a lemon cell, which parts are the electrodes and which is the electrolyte?
Copper wire and iron nail are electrodes; lemon juice is the electrolyte.

Effects of Force
A force can move an object from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion or change its shape — or several of these ...
Contact Forces and Muscular Force
Contact forces act only when objects touch, directly or through a stick or rope; muscular force — from our muscles — is one of ...
Friction
Friction acts between surfaces in contact when an object moves or tries to move; it opposes the motion and is larger on rougher ...
Non-contact Forces and Magnetic Force

items: A force is a push or a pull on an object that comes from its interaction with another object; it is measured in newton (N).
At least two objects must interact for a force to come into play.
Each interacting object feels a force; when the interaction stops, the force disappears.
A force can move an object from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion or change its shape — or several of these together.
No change in speed, direction or shape takes place without a force.
An object at rest may still have forces on it — they balance one another (more in higher grades).
A force may cause some or all of these effects at once.
Contact forces act only when objects touch, directly or through a stick or rope; muscular force — from our muscles — is one of them.
Friction acts between surfaces in contact when an object moves or tries to move; it opposes the motion and is larger on rougher surfaces.
Some forces act without contact; magnetic force — the force of a magnet on another magnet or a magnetic material — is one of them.
Rubbing certain materials builds static charges; a charged body pulls or pushes other bodies without touching them — the electrostatic force.

The Earth pulls every object towards itself without touching it; this gravitational force (gravity) is always attractive.

items: Pressure is the force acting on each unit of area (P = F ÷ A). The same force presses harder on a small area and gently on a large one.
Pressure = Force ÷ Area
SI unit: N/m² = pascal (Pa)
Smaller area → higher pressure; larger area → lower pressure
Liquids exert pressure. It grows with the height of the liquid column (not with the amount of liquid) and acts in all directions — on the bottom and on the walls.
Liquids exert pressure in all directions
Pressure increases with the height of the liquid column
Same height → same pressure, whatever the width
The air around the Earth presses on every object in all directions — this is atmospheric pressure. It is very large, but we are not crushed because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.
Air exerts pressure on all objects, in all directions
Atmospheric pressure is very large
Practical units: millibar = hectopascal = 100 Pa
Wind is air moving from a region of high air pressure to a region of low air pressure; the bigger the pressure difference, the faster it blows.
Air moves from high pressure to low pressure
The flow stops when pressures become equal
Bigger pressure difference → faster wind
Fast-moving air has a reduced pressure, so the slower air around it, at higher pressure, pushes things towards it — that is how storms lift roofs.
High-speed air has low pressure
Higher pressure around pushes objects towards the fast air
Reduce the pressure difference: open windows, holes in banners

Heated land makes warm, moist air rise, leaving low pressure; cooler air flows in, heats and rises too — a continuous circulation. The rising air cools, its moisture forms clouds and rain. Strong winds with rain make a storm.
Warm air rises → low pressure
Cooler air rushes in → circulation
Rising air cools → clouds → rain, hail or snow
Storm = strong winds + rain

Strong up-and-down winds in tall clouds rub ice particles and water droplets, separating charges. When the charges grow so large that air stops insulating, they flow suddenly — lightning; the heated air expands with a bang — thunder. A storm with lightning and thunder is a thunderstorm.
Thunderstorms need moisture and strong winds
Rubbing of ice and droplets separates charges
Huge charges break down the insulating air → lightning
Lightning heats air → thunder

A cyclone is a large spinning system of clouds, winds and rain that forms over warm ocean water: heat released by condensing vapour keeps lowering the pressure, air rushes in, and Earth's rotation spins it round a calm, lowest-pressure eye.
Forms over warm ocean water
Winds much faster than in regular thunderstorms (Amphan 270 km/h)
Condensation releases heat → air rises more → lower pressure
Earth's rotation makes it spin
Wrong: A heavier load always hurts more; pressure depends only on the force. Right: Two equal weights can hurt differently — pressure also depends on the area the force acts on
Wrong: More water (a wider pipe) gives more pressure at the bottom. Right: Act 6.1: equal heights give equal bulges — only the height of the column matters
Wrong: Air has no weight and pushes on nothing. Right: Act 6.3: air pushes on the sheet; the bigger the sheet, the bigger the push
Wrong: Wind blows from low pressure towards high pressure. Right: It always moves from high to low, like air rushing out of a balloon
Wrong: Blowing between two balloons pushes them apart. Right: They move together — the fast air between them is at low pressure
Wrong: Any strong wind is a storm. Right: A storm is strong winds accompanied by rain

sol_items: Connected vessels P, Q, R filled from R: The water rises to the same level in all vessels.
Sucker M on a smooth surface, N on a rough surface: M sticks, since no air can enter on a smooth surface.
More pressure on the ground floor from a roof tank: Raise the tank higher, because pressure increases with the height of water.
Narrow vessel A and wide vessel B at the same leve: Pressure at the same depth is equal (PA = PB), but the force on the base is more in the wider vessel (FB > FA).
Liquids exert pressure only at the bottom: False; they press on the sides also.
Weather is stormy at the eye of a cyclone: False; the eye is calm.

items: Any piece of matter — chalk, sugar, sand — is made of a huge number of extremely small constituent particles, with spaces between them.
Matter is made of extremely small particles.
Grinding or dissolving only breaks matter into smaller pieces / its particles — it stays the same substance.

notes.h: Interparticle Attraction — What Decides the State
items: Particles are held together by attractive forces; their strength depends on the nature of the substance and on how far apart the particles are, and it decides whether matter is solid, liquid or gas.
Interparticle attraction holds particles together.
Strength depends on the substance and on interparticle distance.
Farther apart → much weaker attraction.
The strength of attraction decides the state.

In solids, particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions by very strong attraction, so solids have a definite shape and volume; heating makes them vibrate harder until they melt at the melting point.
Definite shape and volume.
Tightly packed, very strong attraction, only vibrations.
Heating → stronger vibrations → melting at the melting point.

Liquid particles are close but can move past each other within a limited space, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; on heating it boils at its boiling point, and it evaporates slowly at all temperatures.
Fixed volume, no fixed shape.
Particles move within a limited space; attraction slightly weaker than in solids.
Boiling point: fast vapour from inside too; evaporation: slow, surface, any temperature.
Gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction, so a gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills all the space it gets; liquids and gases both flow and are called fluids.
No fixed shape or volume.
Particles move freely in all directions; attraction negligible.
Liquids + gases = fluids.

notes.h: Interparticle Spacing in the Three States
items: Gases have a lot of space between particles and can be compressed; liquids have a little space (sugar fits in) but are practically incompressible; solids have the least — and the spaces contain nothing, not even air.
Spacing: gas > liquid > solid.
Gases compress; liquids are practically incompressible.
Dissolved particles fill interparticle spaces; insoluble sand just adds volume.
Interparticle spaces are empty.
Particles of liquids and gases are always moving; they hit other particles and spread them (diffusion of colour and smell), and they move faster when heated.
Particles of liquids and gases are in constant motion.
Moving particles hit and spread other particles.
Heat → faster movement → faster spreading.

notes.h: Particle Nature of the Three States — Summary
items: Solid, liquid and gas differ in interparticle spacing, packing, attraction and movement — and these explain their shape and volume.
Solid: minimum spacing, closely packed, maximum attraction, only vibrations → fixed shape and volume.
Liquid: slightly more spacing, slightly weaker attraction, move in limited space → fixed volume, no fixed shape.
Gas: maximum spacing, negligible attraction, move everywhere → no fixed shape or volume.
Wrong: A grain of sand or a speck of chalk powder is the smallest unit of the rock or chalk. Right: Each grain is still made of a huge number of constituent particles
Wrong: Particles stay together because they are glued or packed by air. Right: They are held by attractive forces between the particles themselves
Wrong: Particles in a solid do not move at all. Right: They vibrate (move to and fro) about fixed positions but cannot move past each other
Wrong: When water takes a new shape its volume changes too. Right: The shape changes, the volume stays 200 mL
Wrong: A gas stays in the part of the jar where it was put. Right: It spreads to fill the whole space — no fixed volume
Wrong: The spaces between particles are filled with air. Right: They contain nothing at all

sol_items: Why can we pile up stones or sand but not water?: Solids keep their shape; water flows because its particles move over each other.
Why does water take the shape of folded hands but lose ...: Liquids take the shape of the container and flow when not held.
How does air add weight to an inflated balloon?: Air is matter and has mass.
Is a grain of sand the smallest unit of a rock?: No, it can be broken into still smaller particles.
Are the units of chalk obtained by grinding the smalles...: No; they are still chalk made of many tiny particles.
Where did the sugar go on dissolving in water?: It broke into tiny particles that spread in the water.

notes.h: What Is a Mixture? Uniform and Non-uniform
items: A mixture is two or more substances mixed so that each keeps its own properties and they do not react. If its components can be seen it is non-uniform; if they are evenly spread and cannot be told apart it is uniform.
Mixture = 2+ substances mixed; each keeps its properties; no chemical reaction
Non-uniform: components visible; uniform: components evenly spread and cannot be told apart
Alloys (stainless steel, brass, bronze) are uniform mixtures of metals

Air is a uniform mixture of gases — mainly nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Lime water shows the carbon dioxide; dust can be suspended in it but is a pollutant, not a part of air.
Air is a uniform mixture: nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour
Lime water turning milky shows CO₂ in air
Dust is suspended in air as a pollutant, not a part of air

notes.h: Types of Mixtures by Physical State
items: Mixtures can also be named by the physical states of their components — gas and gas, gas and liquid, solid and gas, liquid and liquid, solid and liquid, solid and solid — and each can be uniform or non-uniform.
Name a mixture by the states of its components: six pairs in Table 8.1
Group them by what the components are mixed into: a gas, a liquid or a solid
The state pair does not decide uniformity — check if components can be seen

In common usage 'pure' means not adulterated; in science a pure substance has no other substance in it — it is made of the same kind of particles and cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by any physical process.
Common 'pure' = unadulterated; scientific 'pure' = one substance only
Pure substance: same kind of particles; not separable by any physical process

Passing electricity through water gives hydrogen and oxygen — two substances that cannot be broken down any further. Such pure substances are elements: made of identical atoms, the building blocks of all matter, grouped as metals, non-metals and metalloids.
Element: cannot be broken into simpler substances; made of identical atoms
Water → hydrogen (pop test) + oxygen (brighter flame) — a chemical change
Elements: metals, non-metals, metalloids; 118 known, most solid, 11 gases, 2 liquids

A compound forms when different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio to make something entirely new — with properties unlike its elements, and elements that cannot be separated by physical methods. Water, common salt and sugar are compounds.
Compound: different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
New properties; elements not separable by physical methods
Water (H : O = 2 : 1), sodium chloride (1 : 1), sugar (C, H, O)

notes.h: Mixture vs Compound: Iron and Sulfur
items: The same iron and sulfur give a mixture when just mixed (Sample A: parts visible, iron pulled out by a magnet, hydrogen with acid) and a compound when heated (Sample B, iron sulfide: uniform black, not magnetic, hydrogen sulfide with acid).
Mixture: parts keep properties, can be separated physically (magnet)
Compound: new substance, new properties, cannot be separated physically
Iron + sulfur → (heat) → iron sulfide

notes.h: Uses of Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
items: Elements, compounds and mixtures are all around us, and knowing how they are built lets chemists make medicines and fertilisers and engineers design materials like stainless steel and graphene aerogel.
Elements: iron, aluminium in construction
Compounds: water, medicines, vaccines, fertilisers
Mixtures: air, alloys, wood, steel, concrete; Dhokra uses brass/bronze

Mineral: natural solid, fixed composition
Native minerals = elements; most minerals = compounds
Rocks = mixtures of minerals

notes.h: What Is Matter? Elements, Compounds and Mixtures — Summary
items: Matter is everything that has mass and takes up space; it is either a mixture or a pure substance, and pure substances are elements or compounds. Light, heat, electricity, thoughts and emotions are not matter.
Matter → Mixture | Pure substance → Element | Compound
Physical methods separate mixtures; chemical methods break compounds; elements cannot be broken down
Light, heat, electricity, thoughts are not matter
Wrong: In a mixture the substances react and turn into a new substance. Right: The components only mix — they do not react, and each keeps its own properties
Wrong: Air is a single gas. Right: Air is a uniform mixture of several gases
Wrong: Mixtures are only solids mixed together. Right: Components can be in any state — gas and gas (air), gas and liquid (soda water), liquid and liquid (vinegar) and so on
Wrong: 'Pure' on a label means it is a pure substance in science. Right: The label only means unadulterated; the product (milk, ghee, spices) can still be a mixture
Wrong: Boiling or freezing water breaks it into hydrogen and oxygen. Right: On heating or cooling the water particles stay the same; passing electricity breaks water into hydrogen and oxygen
Wrong: A compound shows the properties of the elements in it. Right: A compound has new properties — hydrogen burns and oxygen supports burning, yet water puts out fire

If water were a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen: Life would be very different, as water would not be a liquid and would not put out fire.

items: The bright part of the Moon seen from Earth changes shape from day to day — these are the phases. It shrinks from full Moon to new Moon (waning, Krishna Paksha) and grows back (waxing, Shukla Paksha); one full cycle takes about a month.

Full → new: waning (Krishna Paksha); new → full: waxing (Shukla Paksha)
Full Moon to full Moon takes about a month

The Moon's shape never changes. The Sun always lights the half of the Moon facing it; as the Moon revolves around the Earth, we see a different fraction of that lit half — that change causes the phases.
Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun
We see only the lit part that faces Earth
Gibbous = more than half of the lit portion; crescent = less than half
Full Moon farthest from the Sun in the sky, new Moon closest

The phase tells where and when to look: the full Moon is opposite the Sun; as it wanes it comes closer to the Sun in the sky; a waxing Moon is easiest at sunset and a waning Moon at sunrise. The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day because it moves ahead in its orbit while Earth turns.
Waxing Moon — look at sunset; waning Moon — look at sunrise
Full Moon is opposite the Sun; new Moon is with the Sun
Moon rises ~50 min later every day

notes.h: Day, Month and Year from Sky Cycles
items: Three natural cycles give three units of time: Earth's rotation makes the Sun return to its highest point — a day (mean solar day, 24 h); the Moon's phases repeat in about 29.5 days — a month; Earth's revolution around the Sun brings one cycle of seasons in about 365¼ days — a solar year.
Day ← Earth's rotation (24 h)
Month ← Moon's phases (29.5 days)
Year ← Earth's revolution and seasons (365¼ days)
Sun highest = shortest shadow

Ancient people noticed about 12 Moon cycles fit in one cycle of seasons. A lunar calendar has the day as the shortest unit, months of about 29.5 days and a year of 12 lunar months (354 days). Because the seasons repeat in about 365 days, they do not stay with the same lunar months.
Lunar month ≈ 29.5 days
Lunar year = 12 months = 354 days
Falls ~11 days short of the seasons each year

Farmers needed to know when seasons arrive, so solar calendars match the year to the cycle of seasons. In the Gregorian calendar the months (30, 31, Feb 28) add to 365 days; the extra quarter day each year adds up to one day in 4 years, so a leap day (29 February) is added in years divisible by 4 — skipped in century years unless divisible by 400.
Solar calendar follows the seasons
Months add up to 365 days
Leap day every 4 years (Feb 29)
Century years leap only if ÷ 400

A luni-solar calendar counts days and months by the Moon's phases but stays with the seasons: the 11-day yearly shortfall builds up to nearly a month in 2–3 years, so an extra month (Adhika Maasa, intercalary month) is added. Such calendars are used in many parts of India.
Moon for months, Sun for the year
11-day gap → extra month every 2–3 years
Adhika Maasa = intercalary month
Amant ends on new Moon; Purnimant on full Moon

The Indian National Calendar is a solar calendar of 365 days, used with the Gregorian calendar for official purposes. It starts on 22 March (day after the spring equinox); months have 30 or 31 days with traditional names; in a leap year Chaitra gets 31 days and the year starts on 21 March.
Solar, 365 days
Starts 22 March (21 March in leap year)
In a leap year, late Phalguna to end of Chaitra shift by one Gregorian date (added)
Month 1: 30, months 2–6: 31, months 7–12: 30

Solar sidereal festivals (Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Bihu, Vaisakhi …) fall on nearly the same date.
Moon-phase festivals change Gregorian dates
Luni-solar shift < 1 month; lunar festivals move through all months
Solar sidereal festivals stay nearly fixed

Artificial satellites are human-made objects launched from Earth that orbit it periodically — most about 800 km up, once every ~100 minutes. They help in communication, navigation, weather monitoring, disaster management and scientific research.
Moon = natural satellite; artificial = man-made
~800 km up, ~100 min per orbit — periodic
Uses: communication, navigation, weather, disasters, research

One change spreads along feeding links
Remove a predator → its prey rises; remove a prey → its predator falls
Balance is dynamic and can be disturbed by natural or human-made changes

All living beings with the places where they live make the biosphere; plants, animals and decomposers depend on one another.
Atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere support and affect one another; life survives because everything works together in balance.
Life survives not because of one thing but because everything works together in balance.
Preserving clean air, water, soil and all forms of life keeps Earth healthy.
Reproduction keeps every kind of living being going; parents pass on genes (instructions) that give similarity, and small changes in them give variation that helps life adapt.
In asexual reproduction one parent makes exact copies: plants by vegetative propagation from leaf, stem or root; microbes and simple animals by splitting, budding or regrowing from parts.

In sexual reproduction two parents each make gametes with half their genetic material; when gametes join, the new cell has a full set — and because each gamete carries a different mix, every child is unique.

In flowers, pollen (male) reaches the ovule (female) by pollination; the gametes fuse in fertilisation to form a zygote; the ovule becomes the seed (with the embryo from the zygote inside), and the fleshy part around the ovule becomes the fruit. (The book simplifies: it calls pollen and ovules the gametes and says the zygote becomes the seed.)

Animals make sperm and eggs; in fish and frogs fertilisation and development happen in water; in birds and mammals fertilisation is inside the female — birds then lay the egg with stored food, while most mammals grow the embryo inside the mother.

Burning fossil fuels releases extra greenhouse gases faster than nature can absorb them; the extra trapped heat causes global warming, which drives climate change — one of the triple planetary crisis.
When natural habitats are destroyed, plants and animals disappear and food chains weaken; every living thing has a role, and diverse ecosystems are stronger.
Pollution of air, water and soil harms people, crops, aquatic life and food chains; it can be reduced by cleaner energy, better waste management and sustainable farming.

All Earth systems are connected, so protecting life needs action at every level — global agreements, cleaner energy, preserving biodiversity, sustainable use by communities, and everyday reuse, repair and recycling.
Hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere and geosphere are connected — damage to one affects the others.
Sustaining life needs action from all — local communities to global leaders.
Wrong: Life is found all through the Earth, deep inside too. Right: All life is found in the thin crust at the surface — as thin as an apple's skin compared to the whole Earth
Wrong: The planet closest to the Sun must be the hottest. Right: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat
Wrong: Any water — even ice — is enough for life. Right: Life needs LIQUID water; the habitable zone is defined by water staying liquid
Wrong: Distance from the Sun is the only reason Earth supports life. Right: Size matters too: the right gravity holds the atmosphere
Wrong: The greenhouse effect is always harmful. Right: A mild greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for liquid water — only EXTRA greenhouse gases cause global warming
Wrong: Earth's magnetic field is only useful for compasses. Right: It shields Earth by pushing away harmful particles that would damage the atmosphere

sol_items: Do planets get colder with distance from the Sun? Why i...: Generally yes; Venus is hottest because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

What if the Earth were too small or too big?: Too small: gravity cannot hold the atmosphere; too big: heavy gases and very strong gravity.
Does the Earth's magnetic field help life?: Yes, it shields us from harmful charged particles from the Sun.

imp_items: Which planets are rocky?
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
What would happen to Earth's oceans if Earth moved much closer to the Sun?
They would evaporate — too hot for liquid water.
What would happen to the atmosphere of a much smaller Earth of the same density?
Its weaker gravity could not hold the gases — they would escape into space.
Why hasn't the oxygen in the air run out although all living beings breathe it?
Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis.
Which is an example of geodiversity: bird songs, mountains and deserts, monsoon weather, or kinds of fish?
Different landforms like mountains, valleys and deserts.
What happens to nutrients in a dead leaf?
Decomposers break it down and return the nutrients to the soil.
